intro: Loops repeatedly update program state. Learn when while, do-while, and for execute, and prove that their bounds, updates, and termination match the intended algorithm.
outcomes: State a loop invariant and termination argument.
Use break and continue without losing updates.
prerequisites: A loop body is a repeated statement or block. An iteration is one execution of the body. An invariant is a property that holds at a chosen point on every iteration.

sections.title: 1. Three loop forms
paragraphs: while checks before the body and may execute zero times. do-while checks after the body and executes at least once; its trailing semicolon is required. for(initialisation; condition; update) performs initialisation once, then checks, executes the body, and updates repeatedly.

Use for for a clear counted traversal, while when a condition governs an unknown number of repetitions, and do-while when one action must occur before checking. These are design preferences rather than restrictions on what each loop can express.
The update must move state toward termination. for(int i=0; i<n; ++i) visits indices 0 through n-1 for a nonnegative n. Using <=n visits one extra value and is wrong for an n-element array.
example: Before the sum loop, sum=0. After bodies at i=1,2,3,4,5, sum is 1,3,6,10,15. The next test at i=6 fails. Output begins sum=15, followed by the countdown 3 2 1.

This fixed small range is safe. Generalising to large n requires checking both accumulation overflow and the final increment. n=INT_MAX makes ++i overflow at the last iteration of this particular <= loop.

sections.title: 2. Invariant and termination reasoning
paragraphs: For the sum loop, just before a condition check with index i, sum equals 1+...+(i-1). Initialisation establishes this at i=1. Adding i and then incrementing i preserves it. On exit at n+1, sum equals 1+...+n, provided all arithmetic is representable.

A termination measure is a quantity that moves toward a limit. For a bounded array traversal, remaining elements n-i decreases each iteration. Proving progress alone is insufficient if arithmetic can overflow or the bound can change unexpectedly.

The sum loop performs n body executions for nonnegative n and constant extra storage: time grows linearly and auxiliary storage stays constant. This is the foundation of later complexity analysis. A closed formula can reduce work but needs its own overflow reasoning.

sections.title: 3. Nested loops, break, and continue
paragraphs: Nested loops multiply work when each outer iteration runs a full inner traversal. Visiting r rows and c columns takes r*c element visits. A triangular loop with inner counts 1,2,...,n instead totals n(n+1)/2 visits.

break exits only the innermost enclosing loop or switch. continue skips the remaining body; in a for loop the update expression still executes. In while, an update below continue is skipped, potentially creating an infinite loop.

Test zero iterations, one iteration, ordinary counts, and the largest supported count. A sentinel loop stops when a special value arrives; define whether the sentinel contributes to the result and how end-of-input is handled. Never use an uninitialised value as the first condition.
example: A while loop that says if(i==2) continue; before ++i gets stuck at 2. Move the required update to a guaranteed path or use a for loop whose update still runs after continue.
For a 2-by-3 rectangular traversal, body coordinates are (0,0), (0,1), (0,2), (1,0), (1,1), (1,2): six visits.

revision: Trace tests, body, and update in order.
State the invariant and arithmetic assumptions.
Explain where continue goes in each loop form.

questions.question: Which loop guarantees at least one body execution?
answer: do-while, because its condition is checked after the body. while and for can fail their first condition check and execute no body iterations.

questions.question: How many times does for(i=0; i<4; ++i) execute?
answer: Four times, at i=0,1,2,3. The fifth condition check sees i=4 and fails. Condition checks are one more than body executions for this normal terminating loop.

questions.question: Why is a mathematical invariant alone insufficient for a C proof?
answer: The proof must also establish that C operations are defined: bounds are valid, values are initialised, and arithmetic stays representable. An invariant written over unbounded mathematical integers cannot justify an overflowing signed-int implementation.
